topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Direct and inverse proportion
topic.scope: direct variation, inverse variation, solving problems with each

nodes.name: Unitary method
external_prereqs: division of whole numbers and decimals

nodes.name: Both quantities increase together in direct variation
Increase alone does not imply proportion
Ratio x/y stays same in direct variation
One goes up, other goes down in inverse variation
Inverse is not simply any decrease
Product xy stays same in inverse variation
Find value of one unit first
Inverse unitary: find total work or amount first
Time, speed, workers, and pipes as inverse; cost, weight, distance at fixed speed as direct

misconceptions.statement: If two quantities both increase, they are in direct proportion.
misconceptions.why: Students notice the common direction and ignore whether the ratio stays fixed.
misconceptions.fix: Direct proportion needs the ratio to stay the same. Both can increase without being proportional, like age and height.

probe.question: Rahul is 10 years old and 140 cm tall. At 20 years, will he be 280 cm tall because age and height both increase?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 280 cm, since both increase so they are proportional.

misconceptions.root_belief: same direction of change means a fixed relationship
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' proportional reasoning and illusion of linearity

misconceptions.statement: If the difference between values is constant, the quantities are in direct proportion.
misconceptions.why: Students use additive thinking from whole number work instead of multiplicative thinking.
misconceptions.fix: Direct proportion means the values are multiplied by the same factor, not that the same amount is added.

probe.question: A pencil costs 5 rupees; 2 pencils cost 10 rupees. If 3 more pencils are added, 5 pencils cost how much if we add 3 to the cost?
probe.wrong_answer: 13 rupees, because 3 more pencils means 3 more rupees.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on additive versus multiplicative reasoning in proportion problems

misconceptions.statement: In direct proportion, the difference x - y stays the same.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse constant ratio with constant difference.
misconceptions.fix: In direct proportion, the ratio x/y stays the same; the difference changes as the values change.

probe.question: x = 4 when y = 6. If x becomes 8, what is y if x - y stays the same?
probe.wrong_answer: 10, because the difference of 2 must stay the same.

misconceptions.source_hint: research on additive strategies in ratio problems

misconceptions.statement: In direct proportion, if one quantity becomes 3 times, the other adds 3.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up multiplying with adding the multiplier.
misconceptions.fix: If one quantity becomes 3 times, the other also becomes 3 times, so it is multiplied, not added.

probe.question: 4 kg of apples cost 200 rupees. What do 12 kg cost?
probe.wrong_answer: 203 rupees, since 12 is 3 times 4 so add 3.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: If one quantity increases and the other also increases, the relationship must be direct proportion and the ratio need not be checked.
misconceptions.why: Textbook examples are mostly clear direct cases, so students skip verification.
misconceptions.fix: Always check that the ratio of corresponding values is the same before calling it direct proportion.

probe.question: Is the table x: 1, 2, 3 and y: 2, 3, 4 direct proportion?

misconceptions.root_belief: looking similar is enough to confirm a rule

misconceptions.statement: Inverse proportion means one quantity is negative of the other.
misconceptions.why: Students link the word inverse with opposite sign or additive inverse.
misconceptions.fix: Inverse proportion means when one quantity increases, the other decreases so that their product stays the same. No negative numbers are involved.

probe.question: If x = 5 and y is inversely proportional to x, could y be -5?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: If one quantity decreases when the other increases, they must be in inverse proportion.
misconceptions.why: Students remember only the opposite-direction part of the definition.
misconceptions.fix: Inverse proportion also needs the product to stay fixed. Some quantities fall as another rises without a constant product.

probe.question: Rohit gets 10 gifts in 1 year, 8 in 2 years, 7 in 3 years. Is this inverse proportion since gifts decrease as years increase?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, as years go up gifts go down.

misconceptions.root_belief: same direction of change means a fixed relationship
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' confusion of inverse proportion with any decreasing relation

misconceptions.statement: In inverse proportion, the sum x + y stays the same.
misconceptions.why: Students think a fall in one must be balanced by an equal rise in the other.
misconceptions.fix: In inverse proportion, the product xy stays the same, not the sum.

probe.question: x = 6 and y = 4 are inversely proportional. If x becomes 8, what is y?
probe.wrong_answer: 2, because the sum 10 stays the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: balancing means equal amount lost and gained
misconceptions.source_hint: research on additive reasoning in inverse proportion tasks

misconceptions.statement: In inverse proportion, the ratio x/y stays the same.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the direct proportion rule everywhere.
misconceptions.fix: In inverse proportion, x multiplied by y is constant. A constant ratio is for direct proportion.

probe.question: x = 10 and y = 5 are inversely proportional. If x = 20, what is y?

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar rule works for every situation
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students applying the direct proportion method to inverse problems

misconceptions.statement: In inverse proportion, if one quantity doubles, the other decreases by 2.
misconceptions.why: Students replace halving with subtracting the same number.
misconceptions.fix: If one quantity doubles, the other becomes half, so it is divided by 2, not reduced by 2.

probe.question: 4 workers finish a job in 12 days. How many days will 8 workers take?
probe.wrong_answer: 10 days, since workers doubled so days go down by 2.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The unitary method always means dividing the given value by the given number.
misconceptions.why: Students memorise one step from direct problems.
misconceptions.fix: In direct problems we divide to find one unit; in inverse problems we first multiply to find the total, then divide.

probe.question: 3 pipes fill a tank in 20 hours. How long will 5 pipes take?

misconceptions.root_belief: a memorised procedure fits every problem
misconceptions.source_hint: research on misapplication of unitary method in inverse problems

misconceptions.statement: For inverse problems, divide the given time by the new number of workers.
misconceptions.why: Students pick the division step without finding the total work.
misconceptions.fix: First find total work as workers × days, then divide by the new number of workers.

probe.question: 6 men build a wall in 10 days. How many days will 12 men take?

misconceptions.root_belief: a memorised procedure fits every problem

misconceptions.statement: In the direct proportion equation, the ratio can be set up with the quantities mixed, like x1/y2 = x2/y1.
misconceptions.why: Students do not track which values correspond.
misconceptions.fix: Pair values of the same quantity or matching situation: x1/x2 = y1/y2, or x1/y1 = x2/y2.

probe.question: 2 kg costs 30 rupees. What does 5 kg cost?
probe.wrong_answer: Using 2/30 = 5/y... gives y = 75 but with 2/y = 5/30 gives 12, treating either as fine.

misconceptions.root_belief: order of terms in a ratio does not matter

misconceptions.statement: For inverse proportion we use the equation x1/y1 = x2/y2.
misconceptions.why: Students use the direct formula by default.
misconceptions.fix: For inverse proportion use x1y1 = x2y2, or equivalently x1/x2 = y2/y1.

probe.question: 5 pipes fill a tank in 12 hours. How long will 6 pipes take?

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar rule works for every situation
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' default use of direct proportion method

misconceptions.statement: Units need not match in proportion problems, so we can mix minutes and hours directly.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the numbers rather than the quantities.
misconceptions.fix: Convert both values to the same unit before forming the ratio or product.

probe.question: A car goes 60 km in 1 hour. How far in 30 minutes?

misconceptions.root_belief: numbers matter but units do not
misconceptions.source_hint: research on neglect of units in ratio and rate problems

misconceptions.statement: More workers always means more of everything, so days taken increase with workers.
misconceptions.why: Students think more people means more of every quantity.
misconceptions.fix: More workers finish the same job in fewer days, so days and workers are inversely proportional.

probe.question: If 5 workers take 8 days, how many days do 10 workers take?
probe.wrong_answer: 16 days, since more workers means more days.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' misclassification of inverse situations as direct

misconceptions.statement: Speed and time for a fixed distance are directly proportional.
misconceptions.why: Students link speed and time as both related to travel without thinking of trade-off.
misconceptions.fix: For a fixed distance, higher speed means less time, so they are inversely proportional.

probe.question: A bus at 40 km/h takes 6 hours. How long at 80 km/h?
probe.wrong_answer: 12 hours, since speed doubles so time doubles.

misconceptions.root_belief: related quantities move in the same direction
misconceptions.source_hint: research on speed-time misconceptions in proportional reasoning

misconceptions.statement: Every word problem with two quantities and a numeric relation is a proportion problem.
misconceptions.why: Students expect every school problem to follow the topic just taught.
misconceptions.fix: Proportion applies only when quantities change by a fixed ratio or product; check with a few values first.

probe.question: A girl is 120 cm at age 8. How tall at age 16?

misconceptions.root_belief: the lesson's rule applies to every problem
misconceptions.source_hint: research on the illusion of linearity in word problems

misconceptions.statement: In direct proportion, a quantity of zero for one variable can still have a nonzero value of the other.
misconceptions.why: Students do not link proportion with starting at zero.
misconceptions.fix: In direct proportion, if one quantity is zero the other is zero too, because the ratio is constant.

probe.question: Cost of pens is directly proportional to number of pens. What is the cost when the number of pens is 0?

misconceptions.root_belief: a starting value can be anything
